## INTRODUCTION
Error signals travel along a single path different from the forward path to avoid ambiguity among choices of error correction. In contrast, neural reentry does not utilize fixed error-correcting functions or paths. It occurs in selectional systems across multiple reciprocal paths. Reentrant neural processes involve the simultaneous exchange of signals in a coordinated manner among multiple dispersed neuronal populations.
## FUNCTIONS OF REENTRY
Such temporally varying patterns of synchronous activity arising among reentrantly linked groups of cerebral neurons can serve to correlate and bind together features present in sensory input signals or in cortically constructed imagery.

# Scientists Discover Atomic-resolution Details of Brain Signaling
*Menlo Park, Calif. —* Scientists have revealed never-before-seen details of how our brain sends rapid-fire messages between its cells. They mapped the 3-D atomic structure of a two-part protein complex that controls the release of signaling chemicals, called neurotransmitters, from brain cells. Understanding how cells release those signals in less than one-thousandth of a second could help launch a new wave of research on drugs for treating brain disorders.

brave-llmcontext.snippet: There is increasing evidence that the brain relies on a set of canonical neural computations, repeating them across brain regions and modalities to apply similar operations to different problems. A promising candidate for such a computation is normalization, in which the responses of neurons are divided by a common factor that typically includes the summed activity of a pool of neurons. Normalization was developed to explain responses in the primary visual cortex and is now thought to operate throughout the visual system, and in many other sensory modalities and brain regions.

brave-llmcontext.title: Signal propagation via cortical hierarchies
brave-llmcontext.snippet:
The wiring of the brain is organized around a putative unimodal-transmodal hierarchy. Here we investigate how this intrinsic hierarchical organization of the brain shapes the transmission of information among regions. The hierarchical positioning of individual regions was quantified by applying diffusion map embedding to resting-state functional MRI networks. Structural networks were reconstructed from diffusion spectrum imaging and topological shortest paths among all brain regions were computed. Sequences of nodes encountered along a path were then labeled by their hierarchical position, tracing out path motifs. We find that the cortical hierarchy guides communication in the network.
## DISCUSSION
In summary, we develop a simple framework to trace communication patterns in brain networks. We show that the putative unimodal-transmodal hierarchy shapes the propagation of signals across the connectome. The present work highlights the importance of considering sequences of nodes encountered during signaling, and the role they might play in network-wide communication.

### Rebrain will take part in the 2026 World Society for Stereotactic and Functional Neurosurgery Congress (WSSFN), held at the Palais du Pharo in Marseille from September 30 to October 3. You will find the team, in the exhibition foyer next to the main entrance.

### Born from academic research and clinical practice, Rebrain is driven by one conviction: improving DBS outcomes also depends on the ability to define a precise, individualized, reliable and reproducible target for each patient. At WSSFN 2026, we will share the next chapter of this journey.

A second expert view on targeting

### Visit our stand to discover how Rebrain’s technology supports patient-specific targeting while complementing the neurosurgeon’s expertise. Combining clinical data and supervised metamodels, it provides a second expert view designed to make targeting decisions more precise, individualized and reproducible, for deep brain stimulation as well as lesioning procedures.

### Members of the Rebrain team – Emmanuel Cuny, Nejib Zemzemi, David Caumartin, Paolo Dos Santos, Pedro Pelejão, Matt Suminski, Randy Jordan, and Lilou Marchand – will be present throughout the congress to walk you through the approach and discuss your own cases.

We take iEEG itself as that source, and give a deliberately simple answer to how this help can be realized. We fit a signal-to-signal model on iEEG alone and freeze it, then insert it upstream of any downstream scalp-EEG model as a fixed transformation. Within the model, each signal is routed through a finite discrete codebook. Because that codebook is fit on iEEG and has finite capacity, every input processed by the model must be re-expressed as a sequence of cortical-signal atoms drawn from an iEEG-learned vocabulary, and content inconsistent with that vocabulary receives no efficient encoding and is attenuated on reconstruction. Applied to a scalp EEG signal, the frozen model does not filter named artifacts but re-expresses it through the iEEG-defined representation. We call this operation cross-modal reprogramming and the frozen model an unpaired cross-modal prior, and we instantiate it as ReBrain, a channel-agnostic model that reprograms each channel independently and so applies unchanged across the heterogeneous montages of both modalities. As Figure 1 shows, this improves the host on recordings from all four hospitals, whereas the same model fitted on scalp EEG instead of iEEG does not, placing the gain in the intracranial corpus rather than the architecture itself.

keenable.title: NeurIPS Oral Learning Sparse Semantic-Cortical Atoms for Multisubject Naturalistic fMRI Encoding
keenable.snippet: We introduce a multisubject coupled sparse autoencoder that jointly reconstructs language-model features and predicts subject-specific brain responses, learning a sparse basis of semantic-cortical atoms that makes semantic structure, cortical organization, and cross-subject correspondence explicit within a single model. In naturalistic story-listening fMRI, the model retains 88\% of matched dense-feature ridge brain prediction performance using 50 atoms and $k{=}5$ active atoms per TR. Relative to matched two-stage baselines, joint training yields the strongest overall tradeoff between prediction and interpretability. # ReBrain: Brain MRI Reconstruction from Sparse CT Slice via Retrieval-Augmented Diffusion  
### Abstract  
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) plays a crucial role in brain disease diagnosis, but it is not always feasible for certain patients due to physical or clinical constraints. Recent studies attempt to synthesize MRI from Computed Tomography (CT) scans; however, low-dose protocols often result in highly sparse CT volumes, making accurate reconstruction of the full brain MRI volume particularly challenging. To address this, we propose **ReBrain**, a retrieval-augmented diffusion framework for cross-modal brain MRI reconstruction. Given any 3D CT scan with sparse slices, we first employ a Brownian Bridge Diffusion Model (BBDM) to synthesize MRI slices from the available CT data. Simultaneously, we retrieve structurally and pathologically similar CT slices from a comprehensive prior database via a fine-tuned retrieval model. These retrieved slices are used as references, incorporated through a ControlNet branch to guide the generation of intermediate MRI slices and ensure structural continuity. We further account for rare retrieval failures when the database lacks suitable references and apply spherical linear interpolation to provide supplementary guidance. Extensive experiments on SynthRAD2023 and BraTS demonstrate that ReBrain achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-modal reconstruction under sparse conditions. The code will be released upon acceptance.

Similarly, a network of interconnected synfire chains can account for key experimental findings in free monkey scribbling with respect to cortical activity and the statistics of the generated trajectories (Hanuschkin et al., ).
So far, modeling studies have investigated the simultaneous and sequential aspects of compositionality in isolation. However, it has yet to be shown that synfire chains can provide the substrate for compositional systems requiring both computational features, such as motor control. It is not clear that the aspects can be combined, as the models described above that exhibit simultaneity or sequentiality rely on entirely different mechanisms: simultaneity is realized by synfire chain binding, whereas sequentiality is realized by the propagation of activity from the end of one chain to the beginning of the other. It is therefore not obvious that the computational features are compatible either in terms of network architecture or in terms of parameters. Here, we demonstrate that both types of computation can indeed be carried out in a single network model.

Without a solution to the binding problem, we would require brute force enumeration of all possible combinations, which is intractable due to the combinatorial explosion of options (Becke et al., 2015; van der Velde & de Kamps, 2015). When considering all possible combinations for N concepts, there are 2N possible bindings. For example, for only 25 concepts, there are already more than 33 million possible combinations. Given that humans easily have more concepts than that, this approach would quickly exceed the number of neurons in the brain (or, for that matter, the number of atoms in the universe). In particular, this has been a hard problem for connectionist systems, which often struggle with the binding problem and the tractable implementation of compositionality (Fodor & Pylyshyn, 1988; van der Velde & de Kamps, 2006). However, once we have a tractable mechanism for binding, we can effectively repeat the same process to combine the results of previous combinations, leading to recursive compositionality. This implies that the selected solution to the binding problem must be able to handle multiple levels of binding. Recursive compositionality is a key feature of many symbolic systems, notably language, and it allows for the “flexible generation and comprehension of an unbounded number of complex ideas” (Chomsky, 2006; Frankland & Greene, 2019).

octen.title: Leanpub: Publish Early, Publish Often
octen.snippet:
Firstly, given the context of previous activity, the layer of neurons can use predictive inputs to “fill in” gaps in its sensory inputs and compensate for even more missing data or noise. Secondly, at any moment the layer is using the current pattern to predict a set of future inputs, which is the first step in learning sequences.
A layer composed of singe cells is limited to predicting one step ahead. To see why, note that at any time, there is information about the current input, represented by the pattern of firing cells, and also information about what the layer predicts will come next, represented by the pattern of predictive depolarisation in cells connected to the current pattern. Conversely, the predictive pattern is based on information only one step in the past, and the layer can’t learn to distinguish between different sequences where the difference is two or more steps in the past. Thus it “forgets” any context which is more than one time step old.
Clearly, our brains have the facility to learn much longer sequences than this. Most of our powerful abilities come from combining high-order sequences into single “chunks” and thus very efficiently storing rich sensory memories and behavioural “scripts”. So we need to extend our model of a layer to fulfil this important requirement.
The trick is to replace each cell with a column of cells, and to use this new structure in a particular way to produce exactly the kind of high-order sequence learning we seek.

### Abstract

Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is a cornerstone of clinical brain monitoring, making the quality of its signal fundamental to downstream tasks and models. However, that signal is heavily contaminated by non-neural interference and blurred by volume conduction. Existing methods operate almost exclusively within the scalp modality, so they inherit the contamination they would need to overcome. In practice, intracranial EEG (iEEG) observes the neural activity with far higher fidelity, yet it is invasive and therefore scarce, and the two modalities are rarely recorded as pairs at scale, share no common channel space, and offer no clean ground truth to directly supervise a mapping. Motivated by the neuronal synchronization mechanism shared by the two modalities, we propose a reprogramming approach that fits a signal-to-signal model on iEEG alone and freezes it as a cross-modal prior. ReBrain consistently improves host models across recordings from multiple hospitals and across architecture families, and our analysis traces this gain to genuine neural structure carried by iEEG rather than to the architecture itself. This work provides evidence that a scarce clean modality can serve as a transferable prior for an abundant noisy one, offering a general recipe for cross-modal transfer among biosignals. 本研究提出ReBrain框架，将稀缺的高保真颅内脑电图（iEEG）先验迁移至头皮脑电图（EEG），无需配对或微调即可提升临床头皮EEG分析性能，为生物信号跨模态迁移提供通用方案。

## 摘要：

头皮脑电图（EEG）是临床脑监测的核心手段，其信号质量对下游任务和模型至关重要。但该信号受非神经干扰严重污染，且因容积传导而模糊。现有方法几乎仅在头皮模态内运行，因此继承了本需克服的污染。实际中，颅内脑电图（iEEG）能以高得多的保真度观测神经活动，但其具有侵入性，因此数据稀缺；且两种模态很少大规模配对记录，无共同通道空间，也无干净的真值来直接监督映射。受两种模态共享的神经元同步机制启发，我们提出一种重编程方法，仅基于iEEG拟合信号到信号的模型，并将其冻结为跨模态先验。我们引入ReBrain框架，用于将iEEG学习到的先验迁移至头皮EEG，该框架通过该先验重新表达任何头皮信号，可插入任何下游模型的上游，无需配对或微调。ReBrain在多家医院的记录及各类架构系列中均能持续提升宿主模型性能，我们的分析表明，该增益源于iEEG携带的真实神经结构，而非架构本身。本研究证明，稀缺的干净模态可作为丰富的噪声模态的可迁移先验，为生物信号间的跨模态迁移提供了通用方案。我们的代码可在该https URL获取。

## 英文摘要：

Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is a cornerstone of clinical brain monitoring, making the quality of its signal fundamental to downstream tasks and models. However, that signal is heavily contaminated by non-neural interference and blurred by volume conduction. Existing methods operate almost exclusively within the scalp modality, so they inherit the contamination they would need to overcome. In practice, intracranial EEG (iEEG) observes the neural activity with far higher fidelity, yet it is invasive and therefore scarce, and the two modalities are rarely recorded as pairs at scale, share no common channel space, and offer no clean ground truth to directly supervise a mapping. Motivated by the neuronal synchronization mechanism shared by the two modalities, we propose a reprogramming approach that fits a signal-to-signal model on iEEG alone and freezes it as a cross-modal prior. We introduce ReBrain, a framework to transfer an iEEG-learned prior to scalp EEG, which re-expresses any scalp signal through that prior and can be inserted upstream of any downstream model with no pairing or fine-tuning. ReBrain consistently improves host models across recordings from multiple hospitals and across architecture families, and our analysis traces this gain to genuine neural structure carried by iEEG rather than to the architecture itself.

ultimate.title: NeurIPS Oral Learning Sparse Semantic-Cortical Atoms for Multisubject Naturalistic fMRI Encoding
ultimate.snippet: We introduce a multisubject coupled sparse autoencoder that jointly reconstructs language-model features and predicts subject-specific brain responses, learning a sparse basis of semantic-cortical atoms that makes semantic structure, cortical organization, and cross-subject correspondence explicit within a single model. In naturalistic story-listening fMRI, the model retains 88\% of matched dense-feature ridge brain prediction performance using 50 atoms and $k{=}5$ active atoms per TR. Relative to matched two-stage baselines, joint training yields the strongest overall tradeoff between prediction and interpretability. The learned atoms are semantically coherent and interpretable, recover more reproducible cross-subject brain maps than standard post hoc encoding-model analyses, align with large-scale cortical structure from Yeo~7 and Neurosynth, and transfer better than ridge to held-out subjects in the low-data regime. This framework provides a more interpretable basis for cognitive neuroscience analyses of semantic-to-brain encoding by linking semantic features to corresponding cortical response patterns across subjects.

ReBrain is an umbrella term encompassing several technological and algorithmic frameworks for closed-loop, AI-driven neural interfaces and large-scale biologically plausible computing platforms. These include: (1) the neural co-processor paradigm for direct bi-directional brain–machine interaction, (2) high-throughput “brain-like” spiking neuromorphic accelerators, (3) retrieval-augmented generative models for structural brain imaging reconstruction, and (4) semantic brain decoding pipelines from functional brain recordings. ReBrain architectures are characterized by deeply integrated decoding and encoding components, joint optimization of task-oriented objectives, and, where applicable, architectural advances enabling real-time scalability or leveraging large-scale external knowledge.

The central algorithmic object is the Co-Processor Network (CPN), which ingests neural recording features (e.g., spikes, field potentials, or extracted sensor data) and produces optimized, multi-dimensional stimulation patterns (across electrical, optical, or magnetic modalities) for target structures.  ... Yet, nearly a century after the neuroanatomical organization of the cortex was first defined, its basic logic remains unknown. One hypothesis is that cortical neurons form a single, massively repeated “canonical” circuit, characterized as a kind of a “nonlinear spatiotemporal filter with adaptive properties” (1).
In this classic view, it was “assumed that these…properties are identical for all neocortical areas.” Nearly four decades later, there is still no consensus about whether such a canonical circuit exists, either in terms of its anatomical basis or its function. Likewise, there is little evidence that such uniform architectures can capture the diversity of cortical function in simple mammals, let alone characteristically human processes such as language and abstract thinking (2).
Analogous software implementations in artificial intelligence (e.g., deep learning networks) have proven effective in certain pattern classification tasks, such as speech and image recognition, but likewise have made little inroads in areas such as reasoning and natural language understanding. Is the search for a single canonical cortical circuit misguided?

A large and diverse body of evidence suggests that intermittent signaling along reentrant paths is critical to a variety of neural functions in vertebrate brains, ranging from perceptual categorization to motor coordination. Reentry takes on a variety of forms enabling many different processes. These processes facilitate the coordination of neuronal firing in anatomically and functionally segregated cortical areas.
Reentrant neural processes involve the simultaneous exchange of signals in a coordinated manner among multiple dispersed neuronal populations. A second definitional point is largely a matter of taste. While from its inception as a cortical process (Edelman, 1978) reentry was used as the descriptor, other authors have since used different words, such as “recurrent” (Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000), “recursive” (Pollen, 2003) or “top-down” and “bottom-up” (Van Essen, 2005) to refer to the same process.

Abstract. The wiring of the brain is organized around a putative unimodal-transmodal hierarchy. Here we investigate how this intrinsic hierarchical organization of the brain shapes the transmission of information among regions. The hierarchical positioning of individual regions was quantified by applying diffusion map embedding to resting-state functional MRI networks.
Structural networks were reconstructed from diffusion spectrum imaging and topological shortest paths among all brain regions were computed. Sequences of nodes encountered along a path were then labeled by their hierarchical position, tracing out path motifs. We find that the cortical hierarchy guides communication in the network.
A cortical hierarchy is recovered from functional networks using diffusion map embedding (Coifman et al., 2005). The first eigenvector is used to label nodes according to their position in the putative unimodal-transmodal hierarchy (Margulies et al., 2016). Sequences of nodes encountered along a path are labeled by their hierarchical position, tracing out path motifs.
Network communication is undoubtedly shaped by both sets of structures, and future studies should consider subcortical-cortical and cerebellar-cortical signal traffic. In summary, we develop a simple framework to trace communication patterns in brain networks. We show that the putative unimodal-transmodal hierarchy shapes the propagation of signals across the connectome. The present work highlights the importance of considering sequences of nodes encountered during signaling, and the role they might play in network-wide communication.
